ingredients.name: Tuna (yellowfin or skipjack)
ingredients.notes: or any firm fish such as kingfish or sailfish; cut into 3cm cubes

ingredients.name: Goraka (Garcinia cambogia/gamboge)
ingredients.notes: dried pieces, soaked in warm water for 10-15 minutes before grinding

ingredients.name: Roasted curry powder
ingredients.notes: see sl_006 Roasted Sri Lankan Curry Powder

ingredients.name: Curry leaves
ingredients.notes: 3-4 sprigs, plus extra to line the pot

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: for grinding the goraka paste; total liquid about 2-3 cups depending on pan size

steps.instruction: Soak the goraka pieces in warm water for 10-15 minutes until softened. Drain, then grind to a fine paste using a little water to help the grinding process.
Grind the garlic, black pepper, curry leaves, pandan leaf, chilli powder, and turmeric powder together into a fine spice paste.
Combine the goraka paste and the spice paste. Taste and adjust salt and pepper -- the mixture should taste sour, hot, and salty in balance.
Wash and cut the fish into 3cm cubes. Coat each piece thoroughly with the combined paste, being careful not to break the fish pieces.
Line the bottom of a clay pot (or any heavy-bottomed pot) with curry leaves, and a piece of banana leaf if available -- this helps prevent excessive charring and adds aroma.
Arrange the coated fish pieces in a single layer in the pot, without overcrowding. Add the sliced onion, cinnamon stick, and roasted curry powder over the top, along with any remaining paste.

Cover and cook over low heat, without stirring -- shake the pot gently instead if needed to avoid breaking the fish. Cook for 20-25 minutes, flipping the pieces gently halfway through, until the liquid has reduced into a thick, dark, almost dry coating on the fish.

Let the curry sit for a few minutes off the heat before serving to let the flavours deepen. Serve with plain rice, yellow rice, or coconut roti, alongside a dhal or potato curry since this is a dry curry.

source_site: islandsmile.org, cross-checked against hungrylankan.com and foodcnr.com for technique and ingredient consistency
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 3 independent sources, all agreeing on goraka/pepper as the essential sour-spicy core
notes: An ancient preservation technique from Sri Lanka's southern coast -- the goraka acts as a natural preservative, traditionally allowing the curry to be kept at room temperature for up to a week or refrigerated much longer, originally developed for fishing communities needing to store catch without refrigeration. Unlike most Sri Lankan curries, this is a dry, gravy-less dish with no coconut milk. Goraka should not be substituted with tamarind, as tamarind's sourness is sharper and changes the dish's signature flavour; if goraka is genuinely unavailable, increase tamarind cautiously and taste as you go. A simpler 'Southern style' version uses only goraka, black pepper, and salt as the core paste, omitting the curry powder, chilli powder, and onion used in this richer household variant.
